content_voiceover: Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma splits into two clinically distinct entities based on ALK status. ALK positive ALCL, sometimes nicknamed the ALKoma, typically affects young patients and frequently involves extranodal sites, about sixty percent of cases, including skin, bone, soft tissue, lung, and liver. It's ALK positive, CD30 positive, EMA positive, CD25 positive, and CD15 negative. The defining molecular lesion is the t 2;5 translocation producing the NPM-ALK fusion, though variant partners like t 1;2 also occur. Critically, ALK positive disease carries a much better prognosis. In contrast, ALK negative systemic ALCL occurs in older patients, has less extranodal involvement, and favors bone, soft tissue, and skin when it does spread beyond nodes. It's ALK negative by definition, but still strongly CD30 positive, sometimes CD15 positive, and PAX5 negative. There's no consistent cytogenetic signature. Prognostically it falls in between: worse than ALK positive ALCL but still better than PTCL, not otherwise specified, with a five year overall survival around fifty percent.
keypoints: ALK+ ALCL: young age, frequent extranodal disease, t 2;5 NPM-ALK fusion, better prognosis
ALK- ALCL: older age, no specific cytogenetics, poorer prognosis than ALK+
Both are strongly CD30 positive; ALK- may show CD15+ and is PAX5 negative
ALK- ALCL prognosis is intermediate, better than PTCL-NOS, 5-year OS about 50%
keypoint_voiceover: The board level distinction is simple: ALK positive ALCL hits younger patients, carries the t 2;5 NPM-ALK fusion, and has the best prognosis of the peripheral T cell lymphomas. ALK negative ALCL occurs in older patients, lacks a defining cytogenetic marker, and carries an intermediate prognosis, worse than ALK positive disease but still better than PTCL, not otherwise specified.
